bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Workflow analysis documents how work is actually done in an operational system. The practice records real sequences, decision points, deviations, informal adaptations, role-spanning handoffs and workarounds that may not appear in requirements, process documents or user self-report.

The central distinction is between designed workflow and actual workflow. A workflow diagram drawn from requirements or stakeholder interviews describes how the system was intended to operate. Workflow analysis describes how practitioners complete work under real conditions. In complex professional systems, the gap between intended and actual workflow is often the main finding.

## What workflow analysis does

Workflow analysis produces a role-specific map of actual work. It shows where the system supports the work, where the system resists the work, which informal practices have developed to compensate for interface failures and which informal practices preserve operational knowledge that a redesign should not remove.

The practice treats divergence from the designed process as evidence. A parallel spreadsheet, a printed reference sheet, a checklist taped to a monitor or a repeated navigation pattern can indicate that the interface does not support the work as performed. The same artefact can also contain useful operational knowledge that needs to survive redesign.

In multi-role systems, workflow analysis is conducted per role. A scheduler's workflow, a field technician's workflow and an operations manager's workflow are distinct. Aggregating role workflows can produce a composite account that is accurate for none of the roles.

## When workflow analysis is used

Workflow analysis is primarily used during Sandbox Experiments before design decisions are made. It is also used diagnostically in audits of existing systems, where the purpose is to understand what the platform supports and does not support before recommending changes.

Direct observation is preferred when the operational context permits it. In-situ observation can reveal tacit sequences, informal adaptations and rapid decisions that practitioners may not reconstruct accurately in retrospective interviews.

Session recording analysis can substitute for or supplement in-situ observation when direct observation is not feasible. This situation can occur when a platform is already deployed at scale, when the user base is geographically distributed or when the operational context does not permit in-person access. Session recordings capture what users do with the interface, but not the contextual conditions, time pressures or external factors that caused those behaviours.

Session recording analysis is most appropriate when the platform generates sufficient session data and when workaround patterns are visible in interface interactions. Visible patterns can include navigation errors, repeated attempts and unexpected path choices. Patterns that depend on physical or organisational context may not be visible in recordings.

## How workflow analysis is applied

Workflow analysis uses observation and supporting research methods in combination. Interview evidence alone is insufficient for complex professional work because practitioners may not be able to describe tacit routines, rapid judgements or adaptations made under pressure.

In-situ observation records work in the actual operational environment under real conditions. This method can surface checklists attached to monitors, parallel spreadsheets running alongside the system and shortcuts developed under operational pressure. These findings can indicate interface failure or preserved operational knowledge.

Contextual interview asks practitioners to describe work while doing it or immediately after completing a task. Proximity to the task improves the accuracy of the account compared with a separate retrospective interview.

Protocol walkthroughs ask practitioners to describe specific workflows as if teaching them to a newcomer. This method surfaces sequence logic that experienced practitioners may no longer consciously notice.

Documentation analysis reviews existing process documents, training materials and system specifications to establish the intended workflow. The gap between intended workflow and actual workflow becomes the starting point for investigation.

Session recording analysis systematically reviews recorded usage sessions from a deployed platform to reconstruct actual user behaviour at scale. In-situ observation provides contextual depth; session recording analysis provides behavioural breadth. The two methods are complementary when both are available.

The research protocol changes as early sessions reveal patterns. If a workaround appears in the first clinic, workshop or observation session, later sessions can probe that pattern explicitly. Workflow analysis in complex operational contexts does not depend on a fixed protocol when emerging evidence changes what needs to be investigated.

## Outputs of workflow analysis

Workflow analysis produces a documented map of actual workflows per role. The map records sequences, decision points and deviations from the designed flow.

Workflow analysis produces a catalogue of workaround patterns. Each workaround is tagged as either a failure signal, where the system is not supporting what users need to do, or a preservation signal, where the workaround encodes operational knowledge that should be carried forward.

Workflow analysis produces a catalogue of error types. The catalogue identifies recurring failure conditions across the user population, with frequency and, where measurable, the time cost of detection and recovery. Error catalogues inform both error prevention design and error recovery design.

Workflow analysis identifies handoff points where work or context passes between roles. These handoff points are primary failure locations in multi-role systems.

Workflow analysis provides the empirical starting point for microtask analysis and task-criticality mapping. Workflow analysis identifies the boundaries of significant workflows; microtask analysis decomposes them into discrete actions, and task-criticality mapping assesses which tasks carry the highest operational consequence.

## Evidence from documented engagements

### Triopsis workforce management workflow analysis under operational pressure

In the Triopsis workforce management engagement, 3 in-situ observation sessions were conducted under real operational pressure. Schedulers were observed managing weather incidents, crew shortages and overlapping jobs simultaneously.

Self-report interviews had not produced an accurate account of how work was done under pressure. Observation showed that schedulers regularly encountered combinations of exceptions the interface had not been designed for. The gap between designed workflow and actual workflow widened when operational pressure increased, and the system's state communication was insufficient for the rapid assessments schedulers needed to make.

These workflow findings drove a 47-microtask analysis and the redesign of the exception-handling architecture.

### IDEXX Animana workflow analysis across clinics, countries and roles

In the IDEXX Animana veterinary practice management engagement, workflow analysis covered 35 clinics in 3 countries over 2 weeks. The work examined 4 role types: vets, nurses, reception staff and administrative staff.

The research protocol changed during the fieldwork. When handwritten workarounds appeared across multiple clinics, including checklists taped to monitors and printed reference sheets near terminals, subsequent visits explicitly probed those patterns.

The structural finding was that reception and clinical roles had incompatible cognitive requirements that could not be resolved within a single workflow architecture. This finding was not visible from stakeholder interviews and emerged from observing the same system used by different roles under different conditions.

### Gexcon workflow analysis after domain learning

In the Gexcon CFD simulation engagement, workflow analysis included 23 workplace observations and 24 user interviews. Domain learning preceded the workflow analysis because the team needed to become productive CFD users before observing engineers at work.

The workflow analysis showed that Gexcon concentrated all expert activity in a single working environment. This differed from enterprise software that distributes workflow across multiple simpler applications. The finding determined the scope and structure of the subsequent microtask analysis, which documented 102 individual tasks.

### Swiss petrol forecourt workflow analysis under transaction pressure

In the Swiss petrol forecourt engagement, workflow analysis included 40 hours of structured observation, 532 transactions documented and coded, and 36 cashiers observed.

The analysis produced a design standard: an 84 transactions per hour peak rate documented during observation became the condition against which later design decisions were evaluated. The work also documented complex mixed transactions running up to 7 minutes before redesign and catalogued cashier workaround sequences that had developed under peak load.

### WCO/IPM customs intelligence workflow analysis across operational groups

In the WCO/IPM customs intelligence engagement, workflow analysis covered three operational groups: inspection officers, intelligence analysts and rights holder teams.

The analysis confirmed that each group had a different operational relationship to the platform. Parallel spreadsheets and email chains across member administrations were the primary diagnostic signal. The designed workflow was being circumvented because it did not support what the work required.

### Enhesa session recording analysis as the primary workflow research method

In the Enhesa legal compliance platform engagement, 95 session recordings were reviewed. The analysis documented 31 workarounds across four categories and 12 error types with time-to-redress measurement.

Direct observation of Enhesa users in their operational context was not part of the research programme. Session recording analysis substituted for direct observation and produced a behavioural map of how users were actually navigating the platform compared with how it was designed to be navigated.

The workaround catalogue was structured across four categories: Finding legal texts with 8 workarounds, Using legal texts with 17 workarounds, Account settings with 2 workarounds and Other with 4 workarounds. The concentration of 17 of 31 workarounds in Using legal texts was the diagnostic signal because it showed the highest density of compensating behaviours in the platform's primary content area.

The error documentation extended the analysis to 12 error types, each with measured time-to-redress where correction occurred. Known error types included clicking into the wrong legislative text, creating the wrong filter and missing a search result that was present in the system. The time-to-redress measurement added a cost dimension to the error catalogue. In the redesign, 80% of the documented workarounds were addressed.

The 6 user interviews conducted alongside session recording analysis added contextual depth that the recordings could not provide. The interviews supplied motivations, task contexts and domain knowledge levels that helped explain the navigation patterns visible in the recordings.

### Workflow-derived design responses in an industrial automation engagement

In the industrial automation engagement, the client was a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells. Two designed responses came out of workflow findings.

The first response was a collapsible workflow tree for workflows running to roughly a hundred operations, with grouped property sections for parts carrying up to roughly fifty properties. The second response was an NC programme version table recording name, type, version and creation, addressing a documented engineer complaint about not knowing which programme version was current.

These are design responses, not outcomes. The product is in development.

### AIT workflow split based on operating conditions rather than user research

In the AIT heat pump controller engagement, the workflow split was based on a physical operating condition rather than a researched workflow finding. Commissioning was divided into an installer assistant and a separate end-customer assistant because at a building site there is usually no network, so the installer cannot enter a Wi-Fi password and the owner must complete that part later.

This is design reasoning from operating conditions. The AIT engagement did not involve user research.

### Assemblio workflow artefacts built from client material

In the Assemblio engagement for Composer and Smart Viewer, the workflow artefact was two annotated user-flow diagrams: one for the planner and one for the worker. Each diagram carried the use cases served by the flow, Creative Navy's open questions marked as questions and new features marked as new.

The diagrams described the current flow and also held unresolved decisions about the future flow. Creative Navy conducted no user research of its own on this engagement, did not stand on a shop floor and built the flows from client material and client-stated accounts.

### Oceaneering workflow unit found during review

In the Oceaneering hospital dispatch panel engagement, only the client name may be named. The workflow's real unit was not the unit assumed by the interface. Stations were not independent; they sat in lines determined by the direction the vehicle drives in, and every station on a line had to carry the same role.

Changing the front station of a line to receive while the station behind it sends would cause logistical failure. The whole row changes, or none of it does. This surfaced during review rather than in requirements. No dispatch operator was observed and no depot was visited.

### Maritime VTS hierarchical task analysis across operator journeys

In the maritime VTS engagement, hierarchical task analysis covered seven operator journeys: monitoring traffic and maintaining sector awareness; identifying and inspecting a vessel or track; triaging and disposing an operational alert; coordinating and documenting an incident; reviewing past traffic and replaying safely; monitoring source health and assessing impact; and supervisor and shift handover.

Each journey was decomposed into subtasks, decisions, visible states, permitted actions and recoverable interruptions. Normal, ambiguous and degraded conditions were modelled separately.

Cross-journey transitions were modelled explicitly. Each transition retained an origin reference, including source object or alert, sector, active time mode and route back. The operating principle was that switching screens is not itself completion of an operator task.

## Boundaries and limits

Workflow analysis should not treat every workflow artefact as field observation. Assemblio workflow material was built from client material and client-stated accounts. Oceaneering workflow material surfaced during review rather than through observed dispatch operations. The AIT workflow split came from operating-condition reasoning and did not involve user research.

Session recording analysis has a narrower evidential scope than in-situ observation. It shows what users did with the interface, but not the surrounding conditions, time pressure or external factors that shaped behaviour. In the Enhesa engagement, interviews were used alongside recordings to add context that recordings could not supply.

Workflow analysis in multi-role systems should not aggregate roles into a single composite workflow. The practice treats role-specific workflows as separate because different roles may have incompatible cognitive requirements, decision points and handoff responsibilities.

Some documented engagement entries describe design reasoning or designed responses rather than outcomes. The industrial automation engagement describes designs for a product in development, not product outcomes.

## Related pages

Workflow analysis precedes microtask analysis by identifying the boundaries of significant workflows. It precedes task-criticality mapping by identifying the workflows and tasks that need consequence assessment. It also connects to cognitive-load analysis because workflow analysis identifies where cognitive load is highest before the mechanisms of that load are investigated.

Workflow analysis is also connected to workflow and task structure redesign, audits of complex products and research in complex operational contexts. Those relationships describe how the practice contributes to broader design and research work.
